speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I, too, rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. It concerns the construction of the Trident nuclear base in Bangor, Washington, immediately south of the city of Vancouver. In view of the tremendous size of the Trident installation, its close proximity to Canadian territory and the danger to Canadian lives and property posed by the existence of this base in the event of a nuclear fallout
following a nuclear attack and in view of the long standing friendship, close relationship and atmosphere of goodwill between Canada and the United States, which Canada is presently demonstrating by her commitment to spend $1 billion of Canadian tax dollars to prop up the financially-troubled American Lockheed Corporation by its failure to either consult in respect of or protest such construction of the Trident base where Lockheed happens to be the prime contractor, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas):
That this House go on record as condemning the construction of the Trident nuclear base and request the Canadian government to protest to the United States that construction in the strongest possible terms and, to request immediate consultation and discussion with the United States Government.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION BOARD JURISDICTION OF BOARD TO REVIEW PRICING POLICIES OF GOVERNMENT BOARDS AND AGENCIES-GOVERNMENT POSITION
ANTI-INFLATION BOARD JURISDICTION OF BOARD TO REVIEW PRICING POLICIES OF GOVERNMENT BOARDS AND AGENCIES-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. In view of the fact that the pricing policies of the federal public sector have been removed from the direct jurisdiction of the AntiInflation Board, yet the board reports that almost 10 per cent of their complaints involve government matters, can the minister tell the House whether persons affected by federal price increases have any practical opportunity on a day to day basis to appeal the price policies of federal emanations and, if so, to what body?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Finance):
subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION BOARD JURISDICTION OF BOARD TO REVIEW PRICING POLICIES OF GOVERNMENT BOARDS AND AGENCIES-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member's premise is incorrect. The federal government, and indeed provincial government bodies which recover most of the costs of the services provided by way of user charges, are subject to the Anti-Inflation

April 30, 1976
Oral Questions
Board. As the House has been told many times, other federal tribunals such as the National Energy Board and other boards which govern the provision of services to the public are applying anti-inflation guidelines. In the situation where much of the cost is covered by a subsidy from the federal Treasury and only part is recovered by the user charges, the department or the Treasury Board applies the price and income guidelines in determining the extent to which there should be an increase in the user charge.
The hon. member has said very often that there should be a reduction of the federal government expenditure in this country. We have acknowledged that in the sense of saying that the absolute subsidy provided, for example, to the airlines through the air transport charges, should not be increased and where costs go up the user should be expected to pay rather than have the cost borne by the general taxpayer.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTO PACT-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO REDUCE DEFICIT
CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTO PACT-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO REDUCE DEFICIT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I also have a question for the Minister of Finance. Given the report this morning that a body of United States politicians wants to continue with an unchanged Canada-U.S. automotive agreement-not unusual considering that they had a $2 billion trade surplus in their favour for last year-I should like to ask the minister if he would confirm for the House that in the automotive parts trade for the first quarter of this year we are running a deficit of $600 million in automotive parts alone. I believe that to be the case. Would the minister tell the House what plans the
April 30, 1976

government now has to turn around this unacceptable situation.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Finance):
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTO PACT-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO REDUCE DEFICIT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think I should like to confirm the accuracy of the figure, from a purely statistical standpoint. The position taken by my colleague, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, has my support, namely, that his department has been carrying out an analysis on the current situation, both with regard to automobiles and parts, for the purpose of preparing a position for discussion with the United States on the subject of the auto pact.
Incidentally, the United States administration has been engaged in a similar analysis on their side. I think one would have to recognize that political events in the United States during the balance of this calendar year may make it difficult to complete negotiations for any changes in the auto pact.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTO PACT-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO REDUCE DEFICIT
speechtext: For at least three years now the government has been saying that it has been undertaking studies as to what changes, if any, ought to be made in the Canada-U.S. automotive agreement. Would the minister finally give us some deadline for when the studies will be finished? Specifically, can he tell us what the government intends to do to ensure that Canadians get their share of investment which is at least proportionate to our consumption in that industry. Secondly, when does the government finally intend to make the automotive companies in Canada bring down their prices for Canadian consumers to at least the level at which they sell the same cars produced in this country to Americans?

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTO PACT-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO REDUCE DEFICIT
speechtext:
As the hon. gentleman knows, during the history of the auto pact over the past decade there has been a variation of experience. Indeed, up until 1971 the performance of the pact for Canada had been very much ahead and was the subject matter of some complaint by the then secretary of the United States treasury.
As to whether we will give up our careful study of the program, of course we will not. I think it will be important to monitor the effects of the existing arrangements from time to time to make certain that the program is meeting the interests of the two countries. I agree, however, that it is appropriate that the two administrations should be in position to discuss this, to do a perspective on the auto pact and to see the manner in which it should be changed in the interests of both countries.

speechtext:
1.	Did the Secretary-General of the United Nations invite member states to participate in a disarmament conference and, if so, in what manner did Canada respond?
2.	Did Canada suggest items to be included on the agenda of a disarmament conference and, if so, what were they?

speakeroldname: Miss Monique Begin (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: 'DISARMAMENT CONFERENCE
speechtext:
The answer to the first and second parts of the question is as follows: It is assumed that the questions refer to proposals tc .onvene a world disarmament conference. The possibility of convening such a conference has been the subject of several resolutions in the United Nations General Assembly in recent years. The 28th General Assembly in 1973 estab-
Medical Care Act
lished an ad hoc committee to examine all views and suggestions expressed by governments on the convening of a world disarmament conference and related problems.
The 29th and 30th General Assemblies in 1974 and 1975 received reports from the ad hoc committee and requested the committee to continue its work. Canada supported these resolutions and has been a member of the ad hoc committee since its inception. The deliberations and reports of the ad hoc committee have revealed a wide divergence of view among member states about the need for a world disarmament conference, the conditions essential to its realization, its main objectives, its agenda and other relevant considerations.
The Secretary General of the United Nations has not invited member states to participate in a world disarmament conference but has sought their views and suggestions on the convening of such a conference. In reply to a note from the Secretary General in 1975 and on other occasions the government of Canada has expressed its support in principle for the idea of convening a well-prepared world disarmament conference at an appropriate time but has also expressed its belief that it would not be fruitful to begin preparations or set a date for such a conference until there is reasonable assurance that it would in fact lead to concrete progress towards disarmament.
The government of Canada has stated that there can be little assurance that a world disarmament conference would lead to such progress unless all nuclear weapon states are prepared to participate and to assist actively in its preparation. As these conditions are not yet present the government considers it premature to suggest items that might be included in the agenda of a world disarmament conference. All states, however, continue to have the opportunity to express their views in the United Nations General Assembly itself which devotes several weeks each year to the consideration of arms control and disarmament questions and priorities.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to begin by making a comment concerning the order of voting to which Your Honour made reference. As I see it, the four motions before us are to some extent predicated upon the previous one failing to pass. If we look at it from that point of view, I think the motion put forward by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) perhaps should be the first to be considered, because essentially it calls for the complete elimination of the bill. If that motion should not pass, which I do not suppose it will, the next motion would be the one standing in my name, which calls for the bill to expire following a two-year period. That is a compromise which gives the government a little more leeway than the motion proposed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.
If motion No. 1, in my name, should fail to pass, which I expect will be the case by virtue of the government's majority, then motion No. 2, in the name of the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Brisco), could be considered. This is a further compromise which suggests that if motion No. 1 fails to pass, then motion No. 2 would enable the bill to continue to live its terrorizing life, but that orders in council put forward by the government in so far as percentages of increase are concerned in the third and subsequent years would be debated in the House of Commons and indeed voted on and passed before they are made. As I see it, that is the third compromise.
Finally, there is the motion of the minister, which is even less acceptable but which to some extent would improve the bill because it does call for a debate on the order in council and a vote on it, even though it would be a retroactive vote because the order in council would have been passed in any case. At the moment, my feeling is that that kind of motion would improve an otherwise completely unacceptable bill. It is still unacceptable to us, however, because the amendment does not change the essential intent of the bill. But at least it would enable parliament to express some views on the subject and perhaps have a vote, with the possibility of reversing the order in council if it should prove to be unsatisfactory to the House.
One of our main concerns in dealing with this bill is the view of many people that this is but the first step in the desire of the government to back out of its commitment to cost-sharing with respect to medical care premiums, as it is doing in the case of the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act. We have a situation where this government demonstrated extreme arrogance in the first place by introducing this bill in a unilateral way at a time when negotiations between the two levels of government were going on and, second, by its use of closure to cut off the debate on second reading.
Even though the government has a majority in the House at present, by this kind of technique they are abusing that advantage. I do not think the people of Canada felt, when the rule changes were introduced in 1969, that they would result in an abuse of government power. I think the use of closure when it is unnecessary, when members of the House, who represent the people of

Canada, want to express their views on a subject which will in the long run affect every Canadian, should not be employed to close off debate and thereby take away the right of members of the House to speak on behalf of Canadians, whether Canadians as a whole or Canadians in certain parts of the country.
The minister, in spite of the fact that after the debate on motion No.l, which calls for expiry of the bill after two years, the bill may well be unnecessary after a two-year period, still wants it in place because he wants some power. That this bill will give the minister some power is probably the understatement of the year, because that power amounts to a spiked club which can be used to clobber the provinces over the head during the negotiations for the readjustment of cost-sharing arrangements.
Another matter which has concerned me very much, and which has already been referred to on a number of occasions, is that of research. In his statement on the bill before us, the minister expressed concern about the rising costs of health care, but he did not make the slightest suggestion as to how these costs might reasonably be reduced. He simply said that he will just not pay them if they go beyond a certain point, and he leaves it entirely up to the provinces to decide how the service might be streamlined and how the costs might be reduced without the destruction or degradation of the standard of service which is now being provided.
I think the minister's refusal to deal fairly with medical research in this country indicates, perhaps more than anything else, his lack of comprehension of the need for research and of the fact that there is no better way in the world to reduce health care costs than through research of various kinds, even research into how to reduce the cost of research in various disease processes which is now costing a great deal of money. If research produces better answers with regard to the causes and treatment of illnesses, we know that in the long run these costs will be substantially reduced. I could use, as an example, the advent of various drugs used in the treatment of mental illnesses and the result this has had in virtually emptying overcrowded mental hospitals across the country for so many years which were simply providing what was considered as custodial care for people who were not well. Through research, certain tranquillizers have been developed, and the majority of patients who had been in institutions for 20, 30 years, or all their lives, are now functioning in society.
It appears to me that the thinking of the minister, and perhaps even more so of his parliamentary secretary, has been shortsighted in the extreme with regard to health care costs and how they could be reduced through increased assistance to research. We believe, from having observed the minister and his parliamentary secretary, as well as this government as a whole, that they seem to be spending too much time thinking about how to get power and keep it, and they do not spend sufficient time thinking about how to exercise power to benefit all Canadians.
If there is any message I want to leave while I am on my feet on this occasion, it is that this government should not be totally absorbed with the question of taking power and holding it in perpetuity. It should devote at least half its energy and effort in deciding how to exercise this power in
April 30, 1976

such a way that Canadians benefit. When a government decides that a good way to save money in the area of health care costs is by destroying the research capability of this country, if it is not an abuse of power then certainly it is an improper use of power.
Another matter which has arisen as a result of this debate-medical research is certainly tied closely to this whole question-is that there has been no real dialogue between this government and the research community. I think that is a shameful situation, because we know that the research community is in a position to make suggestions to the government, not political suggestions but certainly suggestions on matters which may be very useful in terms of long-term planning when it comes to the relationship of man to his environment, and perhaps long-term planning related to various serious problems facing us today.
We know that the president of France, for example, has breakfast with representatives of the research community on a regular basis, perhaps twice a month. We know that members of the British government have a method of keeping in close touch with the research community of that country. We know that U.S. senators have their own "tamed" scientists, for lack of a better word, who keep them informed on various aspects of research in the country and how scientific information can be used for the benefit of Americans through proper application of funds by whatever government happens to be in power.
Therefore, I would like to emphasize the point that this government is failing the trust which has been placed in it by the people of Canada by neglecting, not only to speak adequately with the research community but, indeed, by destroying that community's position and research programs by putting a freeze on its budgets. I think that is totally unacceptable.
We know that in the scientific community the general policy which scientists follow, no matter in what part of the world they live, is to make their information freely available to scientists in all other parts of the world. It appears, therefore, that the policy of the Canadian government is that we do not really have to do research; we can let somebody else do it, and it is available to us. We can obtain it simply by reading scientific journals. That is the policy of this government. If I had anything to do with it, I would certainly not pursue that kind of policy. If Canadians were aware of the fact that this seems to be the official policy of this government, I think they would be ashamed.
The minister has put forward a couple of amendments. The additional amendment he put forward would result in the situation that after this bill comes into effect, and onward, there will no longer be an 8 per cent ceiling but it will be set by order in council. He put that amendment forward under the guise of improving the bill, but I am not satisfied that it will really improve the situation. As a matter of fact, that kind of amendment leaves the door open for the minister to set the percentage much lower than 8 per cent, and perhaps freezing it, as the government did with regard to the medical research budget. That is of significant concern to me because it will worsen the crisis
Medical Care Act
the provinces may face if the government proceeds with the course upon which it has embarked.
The minister has indicated that motion No. 4 is based on motion No. 2, which was put forward by the hon. member for Kootenay West. That, again, indicates to us in the official opposition the fact that closure is an awful tool; it is destructive, to some extent, of the democratic process. It also indicates to us the usefulness of prolonging a debate ad infinitum if we feel strongly enough about a certain subject or a certain change which may be necessary. I am sure that had we agreed to let this bill pass last fall, the minister would not have accepted any suggestions to change it, least of all one which would allow for parliamentary debate on the order in council setting out the percentage which the minister may want to fix for the third year or after. It shows us that in spite of the fact that hon. members on the other side of the House do not listen very carefully, that their skulls, as I mentioned previously, seem to be very thick and that the noise has to be very loud and long before it gets through, if it is long enough, loud enough and repetitive enough, perhaps it does sink in.
The position we took has been justified. It has been shown that we spoke long enough and loudly enough to try to improve the bill, even though the improvement is very minimal and still does not make the bill any more acceptable in terms of its principle. However, it does introduce an element of democracy and for that reason I am not too unhappy about the amendment.

April 30, 1976
Medical Care Act
The present Medical Care Act calls for the federal government to pay 50 per cent of the costs of medical care which the provinces have to meet. Once this bill is in, there will be two choices. One of those choices hangs on the use of the phrase "the lesser of", so that in the end there is only one choice. The government will pay the lesser of two amounts, either 50 per cent of the total costs of the provinces or only so many more dollars than the provinces got last year. Even when the minister can stand up and talk about hundreds of millions of dollars more, the fact is that that sum of money will be less than would have been the case if this bill had not been brought in. We contend that this is a betrayal of the provinces and of the people of Canada. It is a going back on the principles which were established in the Medical Care Act after all the years it took us to get that legislation.
I join again with the hon. member for Athabasca in registering our protest against this legislation having been put through at the second reading stage by closure, and I join once again in saying that part of the trouble about this whole exercise is that it is a case of how not to conduct federal-provincial relations. The health ministers of the provinces have been most unhappy with the way they have been treated, especially since the announcement by Mr. Turner in the budget he brought down last June. We think the whole story is a sorry mess.
However, we have just about reached the end of the report stage of this bill, leaving the third reading stage to come later, possibly next Wednesday, although I understand that it may be shifted to Thursday, and in this final part of the debate on the report stage I think not only should I direct myself to the amendment proposed by the minister, but that I might once again summarize the choices which are before us right now. We have a government bill which proposes certain fixed percentages so far as the increases which can take place this year and next year are concerned. Then in that bill there is a provision that after that the government has the right, by order in council, to fix the ceilings. They can be anything. There could be consultation, but in the end the government makes the decision. That is the picture. This is a bill that in the first and second years has a precise limit, but in years three, four, five, six, seven and on is subject only to the dictatorial, unilateral decision of the government, which puts it into effect by order in council. That is the bill. I tried, by way of amendment, to kill the bill completely and leave the Medical Care Act as it stands. The voice vote was against my motion, and I suppose that may be the result when the recorded vote is taken.
The next position was that proposed by the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yewchuk), that reluctantly we accept years one and two with ceilings, but that the rest of the bill be cancelled; that there be no Bill C-68 after two years have gone by. That is not as desirable as my position,

namely, that the ceilings should be cancelled altogether, but it is a compromise that we can accept if we must. Again, the voice vote was against the motion and the government has shown no willingness to go the other way.
We come to two more propositions. One was the proposal in the motion of the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Friesen) that a government order in council fixing the ceilings in years three, four, five, six, seven, and so on, not come into effect until parliament has voted on it. Yesterday the majority said no to that as well. We now have the proposal of the minister that the government shall have the right to bring in its orders in council in years three, four, five, six, seven, and so on, and put those into effect right away, subject only to the right of 50 members of the House of Commons to sign a motion which would result in a debate. If that debate were to go against the order in council, then it would have to be cancelled. I make the point, Mr. Speaker, that there is a tremendous difference between having the right to vote on the validity of those orders in council before they are put into effect and simply being given the right to do that after the horse has been stolen, as I said last night.
I think the least acceptable of the propositions is the one before us in the name of the minister. If his proposition carries, we will have a bill that fixes contribution ceilings for years one and two and leaves the government free to fix the ceilings by order in council for all the years after. All that is left for parliament is the possibility of a debate if 50 members sign a motion requesting such debate. So long as the government that brought in the order in council has a majority in the House, it of course can expect to get its order in council approved. Mr. Speaker, I think we are being treated shabbily with respect to this whole matter.
I also want to say, as we have said on occasions similar to this one, that we think it is shabby treatment to say this matter can be debated only after 50 members sign the necessary motion. There are two parties in this House which have fewer than 50 members; we have 16 and the Social Credit party has 11. The "Moncton" party has only one, but he is not here just now. If this kind of motion is going to be made at all, I think instead of it being necessary for 50 members to sign such a motion it should be a number that would make it possible for any one of the recognized parties in this House to bring on a debate by itself. Mr. Speaker, I want to make a few remarks in the debate on the resolution put forward by the minister. Before I do so, however, I should like to speak to the order in which the resolutions are to be voted on next Wednesday afternoon. As I understand it, the matter was taken under advisement by the Chair, and the Chair accepted responsibility by indicating the order.
I also listened to the point of view taken by the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yewchuk). I can indicate that for our part we have no objection to the resolutions being voted on in the order which the hon. member recommended, or in any order which might appeal to the Chair. I want to be reasonable on that matter, as the government has been reasonable on every aspect of this bill which has been put before the House to deal with medicare. There is no doubt that when bills to pay for the programs of the government are put forward, it is the government of the day that takes the responsibility for the way in which the money taken from taxpayers is spent.
Over and over again I have heard hon. members opposite express regret that the provinces will now have to adjust their spending in accordance with the position which may be taken by the federal government, if they expect the federal contribution. No sympathy has been indicated by them for the taxpayers of Canada as a whole and the burden placed upon them by the present arrangements. As the minister has often indicated, these arrangements require the signing of a blank cheque by the federal government year after year for its share of the medicare program.
Blank cheques are fine during the maturing of a new program when medical services were rapidly becoming available for the first time to all Canadians. Surely the time comes, however, when it has to be recognized as a mature program. If it continues to grow at an ever-accelerating rate, it becomes obvious that in the interests of the taxpayers, measures have to be taken to restrain the
Medical Care Act
rate of growth. This fact is recognized not only by this government but by all provincial governments. The Premier of Ontario, for example, has said repeatedly that what is required now are measures to restrain the rate of growth. It is conceded there will be growth next year, the year after, and indefinitely into the future. But how much is not a matter for decision.
I contradict what I think is the most outrageous allegation hon. members opposite have made, an allegation which we have answered repeatedly. I hope this is the last time it will be necessary to repeat that medicare and hospital care programs introduced by this government are programs of which we are proud and for which we intend to take continuing responsibility. But if these programs are to survive it is absolutely necessary for there to be control over how they develop. The hon. member for Athabasca criticized the minister for saying last night that the federal government wants some measure of control over these programs. What is wrong with the people of Canada exercising control over these programs? It is unreasonable to expect the people of Canada, through their elected government, not to exercise control over a mature program.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) objected to the third arrangement as being impractical because no specific figure is assigned. But he also objected to the arrangements for the first two years where specific figures are assigned. You cannot have it both ways. If proper responsibility is to be assumed, you must concede that the federal government must have some say about how much the people of Canada are to be committed to spend on medicare and hospital care. The opposition was irresponsible in alleging that the federal government has no proposals for low cost medicare.

It is of the utmost importance that we as a government, in conjunction with provincial governments across this land of ours, give to these young men and women every opportunity to get into the business of farming. I think we must be very cautious about this question of incentives, particularly as it applies to young farmers, because of the problems there have been with regard to the dairy industry in Canada.
I think in some instances we must look at the incentives that were put forward, both by the federal government and by many of the provincial governments, which have resulted in young farmers, particularly in the dairy industry, becoming involved in a situation from which they will have difficulty extricating themselves. I speak primarily of the young farmers in Ontario who took advantage of the IMPIP loans provided in good faith at that time by the provincial government. This was an incentive program of which many young men and women in my area took advantage. Possibly this was also the case in other provinces which had similar schemes. These young people entered the dairy business because they saw a great future in it. However, by the middle of last year we were confronted with an over-supply of dairy products, particularly powdered milk. Now these people having received the IMPIP or farm credit loan find themselves in a situation where the quotas given to them by the provincial milk marketing boards and provincial governments simply are not sufficient to cover their outstanding payments.
Last night one hon. member brought before the committee a situation involving' a young man who had applied for a Farm Credit loan. His situation was reviewed by the officials of the Farm Credit Corporation who agreed that the loan had been made and that the quota allowed the young farmer would be sufficient to allow him to meet the obligation he would be subjected to under the terms of the loan. Now that the provincial milk marketing board has reduced the quota by 15 per cent, this young man with his sizeable obligation is faced with the payment of a loan in the amount of $900 a month, together with an input loan that would increase the payment by about $300 a month, which would require that he come up with $1,200 each month while being faced with the reduction of the quota in the next coming year. This is the situation which presently exists.
Of course there is mention in the motion that an incentive should be allowed that would entice young people to enter the business of agriculture. While it is all well and good to entice anyone to enter the business of agriculture or to increase his commitment in the field of agriculture, we must also take into consideration the possibility of cut-backs and over-supply because in such a situation we would be enticing people into an occupation in which they would find themselves hard pressed to keep up with it in the future. I think we must give very sincere consideration to this when considering the motion before the House.
The motion suggests that the governement should consider the advisability of amending the Farm Credit Act. Some amendments have been submitted before the agricultural committee and before the House with regard to the Farm Credit Act up to this point, and others certainly will be presented by the government in the future in its

April 30, 1976
Farm Credit Act
attempt to encourage agriculture in the province of Ontario and throughout the Dominion of Canada.
Last night at the meeting of the Standing Committee on Agriculture the question arose about the possibility of farm credit loans approved by the Farm Credit Corporation being extended, or that there be a period of grace for a period of a year or two years in respect of young farmers who have found themselves in the situation I earlier described. I think this is something which could be done without a change in the Farm Credit Act because it is now stated that a farmer, whether he be a young or older farmer, if he finds himself in difficulty can defer payments for a period of one year or perhaps two years. I think that is presently in place in the act and can be considered on an individual basis.
I do not think we should make this a blanket coverage to allow people to defer payments, or that we should make an exception to the over-all rule. I believe it must be considered on an individual basis, and on the understanding that officials of the Farm Credit Corporation will go to the farm involved, take a look at the operation and if possible decide what changes should or could be made under the present confines of the act to allow the producer to meet his commitment.
It also must be pointed out that under the Farm Credit Act the number of defaulters to this point has been very minimal. In fact the number is so low that I believe a great deal of pride should be taken in the fact that the Farm Credit Act has such a very small percentage of its loans that have reached the default stage. It was pointed out on a number of occasions at the meeting last night that several farmers, particularly in western Ontario in the area with which I am sure the hon. member is very familiar, are now bringing to a close mortgages that have been held by the Farm Credit Corporation. Some of these mortgages are at 5 per cent, 6 per cent and 7 per cent. These members of the agricultural community are bringing these mortgages to repayment long before the required time to do so. It is possible that in some instances they would be well advised to invest that money in the banks at a much higher rate of interest so that they would receive a better return.
I am talking about the farmers of Canada. They are people who historically do not like to have a debt of any kind outstanding against them or against their property. I think this is a subject which should be considered in any discussion here in the House of Commons in respect of the agricultural community.
Also at the meeting last night the question of partial payment or advance payment was brought up. The hon. member who introduced this motion most certainly was in attendance and will recall that a statement was made to the committee meeting that pre-payment or advance payment on any of these loans certainly is allowed. The question was raised whether people could, without penalty, make an advance payment on capital on the loans they acquired from the Farm Credit Corporation. We were assured at that time that such a payment certainly could be made without penalty. I think this is something we might take a look at in respect of other areas of the community in relation to mortgages on houses, mortgages on apartments, business mortgages, and business loans because the people in the farming community have some-

what of an advantage in being able to take out a loan and pre-pay it without penalty.
Perhaps we could make a suggestion to people in the housing field that it might not be such a bad idea if the same thing were carried over into housing in Canada so as to allow young men and women, some of whom have taken a very substantial mortgage on the houses which they occupy, an opportunity, if they have had a good year-and we can hope for good years in the future-to advance their payments on those obligations, thereby allowing them to cut down the number of years in which they will be faced with a rather heavy burden in so far as mortgage payments are concerned, but without a penalty involved in that clause. As most hon. members know, at present people who carry a mortgage on a house do so for at least five years with an option at the end of five years either to have the interest on that loan brought up to present standards or, if those standards should decline, lower than present mortgage rates, as we hope they will, to renegotiate the mortgage.
It was pointed out at the meeting last night that under the Farm Credit Corporation Act these mortgages are not renegotiable, in other words the interest rate that is granted on a mortgage under the Farm Credit loan runs for the life of the mortgage. The question was raised by the hon. member-and a very good question too-as to whether we should not look into the future to arrange Farm Credit Corporation mortgages on a five year renewable concept. I have some difficulty in accepting the idea simply because of the most recent experience.
If, in the last ten or 15 years, you had a CMHC mortgage, you would realize that the mortgage rate has always been going up. In the past five or ten years we have never witnessed such a mortgage rate on the decrease. It is hoped that, in the future, high mortgage or high interest rates charged on industrial or housing mortgages will be on the downgrade, but we must also realize that mortgages granted under the Farm Credit Corporation Act, which are now at about 9.5 per cent or 9.75 per cent, are much below the rates that are currently charged on loans for housing. I cannot foresee a decrease in those rates on Farm Credit mortgages, so it might be an advantage to the farmer to have a renewable mortgage after five years. But in general we must accept the fact that in recent history mortgage rates have been rising, so that the farmer who accepts a mortgage at 9.5 per cent or 9.75 per cent under the Farm Credit Corporation Act has a considerable advantage over those who go into the open market and get a mortgage from a bank, a lending institute or a credit union.
The subject of credit unions was also discussed last night and the minister and officials of the Farm Credit Corporation left themselves open to any suggestion that would be put forward by any member of the agricultural committee regarding possibilities of making mortgages available to young farmers at a lesser rate. The rate proposed in the motion is 5 per cent, and I think we will have to give careful consideration before granting a 5 per cent mortgage to farmers when mortgages to anyone else in our society are certainly well above 10 per cent, perhaps even 12 per cent.
April 30, 1976

I am fully in agreement with giving every opportunity and every concession possible to the young farmer, or to the farmer who wants to expand his operation into a more viable business concept, but we also have to take into account in all our deliberations the aspirations of the rest of the Canadian population, of those who are not farmers, of those who are in the cities who are trying to mortgage a house and who have to pay the rate of 12 per cent, and maybe even 13 per cent or 14 per cent, and if they need a second mortgage they have to pay a rate even higher than that. It must be pointed out also that under the amendments to the Farm Credit Corporation Act second mortgages in some aspects of the farming field will be allowed. This also should be considered when comparing the advantages of the agricultural community with some of the disadvantages of other people in this country.
At times we tend to segregate our population into those who are on the farm and those who are off the farm. While there are certain things about agricultural life that we must realize are advantageous, we must also realize that farmers must compete with the rest of society. The general public must also realize that, while the farmer is special in many respects, he is also very different from people in the rest of our community. So we must be very careful about that rate of 5 per cent. I think that in some ways it is too low to be realistic because the interest rates that are asked and received throughout the rest of our society are much higher than the rate suggested in the motion put forward by the hon. member.
With regard to the open-ended loans which will allow additional borrowing without financing charges, I believe the Farm Credit Corporation Act now allows a person to come in with a second mortgage. If he has borrowed, say, $20,000 in the past, and then brings in another application for a loan because he wants to expand his property to make it more viable, the $20,000 is brought into consideration and he is allowed to borrow up to $150,000 if he is under 35 years of age, and still be covered by the Farm Credit Corporation Act. I am not too sure if that is exactly what the hon. member had in mind in presenting his motion, but I believe that this possibility is open to the young farmer or to the not so young farmer, because I think it is important that we take these people into consideration as well.
Another matter that was brought up at the agricultural meeting last evening, and which I want to bring to the attention of the House, is that we must all realize that every segment of our population must take part in the restraint program. It has been said that the restraint program bears down much more heavily on the farm credit aspect of agriculture than on any other segment of our population, and I agree, but it is a fact that the agricultural segment in Canada has always taken a bigger part in Canadian affairs than the rest of our community would like to recognize.
It was pointed out at that meeting that in future young people who wish to apply for loans under the Farm Credit Corporation Act will fall into two groups. Let us say there is a farmer who has a reasonably viable operation, and he has a son who wants to take advantage of the benefits of the Farm Credit Corporation Act. The only way he can take part is to have the loan granted, and the payment is made. Another farmer perhaps has a viable farm business
Farm Credit Act
or farm occupation. He has a couple of sons. I think at the present time what we have suggested is that the Farm Credit Corporation should take a look at that situation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the bill was introduced for the first time in January 1975, there was then perhaps some pertinency. On the other hand, since its original submission in January 1975, the House passed Bill C-34 to amend the Farm Credit Act as attested by the comments of the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Corriveau) who then maintained that the suggested amendments in Bill C-34 would do much towards prompting young people to get involved in farming.
Indeed, Bill C-34 having been passed on May 8, 1975, the Farm Credit Corporation has now almost a year of experience to determine its value. I feel that this motion is out-of-date as a result of the amendments. If you allow me, with my colleagues I would like to examine the amendments to the Farm Credit Act. Now, as we know, the ceiling for loans has been raised from $100,000 to $150,000. If we consider the number of borrowers aged 35 or less, they represented 27 per cent in 1971 and that figure has now reached 43.1 per cent of all applicants taking advantage of the Farm Credit Act. A young farmer under 35 can now borrow an amount over 90 per cent of the productive value of his land, livestock and equipment.
Finally, the New Part IV of the act empowers the corporation to make loans to individuals under 35 whose principal occupation is not necessarily farming, providing that they undertake to set up a farming operation within 5 years. It is a measure that has certainly helped to increase the number of young people to take up farming. Fourthly, the corporation is now empowered to guarantee these loans by way of a mortgage other than a first mortgage.

April 30, 1976
Farm Credit Act
As a result of these amendments, farm loans approved by the Farm Credit Corporation during 1975-76 have reached a record number, while in the previous year they had increased by at least 60.7 per cent, reaching approximately $641 million. Such an increase is mostly due to the amendments. The corporation has made nearly 10,000 loans under the Farm Credit Act. Now, 66 per cent or two thirds of those loans were made to farmers under 35, compared to 53 per cent the previous year and only 36 per cent five years earlier, that is in 1971-72. Under Part III of the act, the corporation lent $318.6 million in farm credit during the fiscal year 1975-76, an increase, Mr. Speaker, of 310 per cent over the previous fiscal year.
The whole amount was loaned to people under 45, since these loans were made under Part II and Part IV of the act. However, in practice, the major part of those funds were borrowed by people, and as I said, under 35. The average amount of the loans made in 1975-76 was almost $65,000, while in the previous fiscal year the total amount was around $50,000. There has already been an increase of $15,000.
In fact, the recent amendments to the Farm Credit Act were intended almost exclusively for young farmers, and they proved so popular that the Farm Credit Corporation had to introduce restrictive credit measures during the current fiscal year in order to retain funds for farmers in greater need. Actually, the motion before us contains four specific measures designed to urge young people to go into farming, such measures supplementing those I have just mentioned.
Under the first measure, the borrower would have part of his loan forgiven provided he met certain predetermined standards of performance. I feel in that respect, Mr. Speaker, that we must take into consideration the rate of repayment by Farm Credit Corporation borrowers in recent years. And on March 31, 1975, as the hon. member who spoke before me indicated, 93.4 per cent of all accounts were up to date, while on March 31, 1976, that percentage had slightly dropped to about 93.2 per cent. It is an insignificant drop if one considers that the beef industry is going through a difficult period and the prospects of the dairy industry are far from being as encouraging as one would like them to be.
Nobody is to blame for this, Mr. Speaker, except the weather which was much more favourable to the dairy production. The corporation has therefore suffered insignificant losses through the years. Given those facts, I think it is useless to dispense the borrowers from repaying part of their loan. Had it been possible to actually prove that the borrowers were having trouble meeting their obligations, the proposed measure might have been advisable.
I feel, like the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), that we have to keep on upgrading the income stabilization programs so that the farmers might meet their actual costs, including the repayment of their loans. In practice, a partial repayment would prove discriminatory. Indeed, the output criterion used to determine this repayment, whatever it is, will always be subject to variables such as the weather, prices and market conditions over which the individual has no control whatsoever and which usually affect the farmers in different ways.

The second measure would establish a 5 per cent ceiling on interest rates. The Farm Credit Corporation rate is 9Vt per cent, and in spite of this, the major challenge the corporation will have to face during this new financial year will be to find enough funds to meet the requirements of the farmers who really need long-term credit.
In my opinion, the ceiling of 5 per cent for the interest rate would only inflate land prices, so that in the end the amounts to borrow and to reimburse would not be lower. In other words, Mr. Speaker, the higher land prices and the attendant increase in loans would largely obliterate the amount saved in interest. In addition, a 5 per cent interest rate would bring farmers to ignore commercial sources of credit and prompt commercial loan companies to withdraw from that market, so that finally less funds would be available to farmers.
The third measure is devised to defer payment of interest during the initial phase of the loan. Now, as the previous speaker has mentioned, it is already possible to defer the reimbursement of principal and interest under the Farm Credit Act and regulations. The reimbursement of principal can be deferred for a maximum of five years, but only for two years as regards principal and interest together. In addition, in practice the corporation can defer payments when it is in the greater interest of the borrower to do so and it takes advantage of that opportunity. It should also be noted that the borrower can make prepayments at any time without being penalized and the interest is later on calculated on the outstanding principal.
Finally, the fourth and last proposal made in the motion would grant open-end loans, that is to say the borrower could borrow again without having to pay refinancing. Thus, mortgages for an undetermined amount would be granted so that farmers could borrow additional funds without having to pay new notary fees and so on. That proposal seems interesting, at first glance. However, after having been studied closely and repeatedly by officials of the department, it was considered not to be practical. Mortgages, as we know, are governed by provincial laws, and no mortgage act mentions mortgages for an undetermined amount.
As we know, a practical solution was found to the problem when the Farm Credit Act was last revised authorizing the corporation to loan money on mortgages other than first. Consequently, when borrowers want to obtain additional funds, they do not have to pay the charges which are normally associated with the title search and to cover the refinancing of the initial loan. They have to pay only the charges associated with the registration of a second mortgage. These charges are not very high in comparison with the average amount of the loan since they only equal less than 1 per cent of the amount of the loan in most provinces. This amendment turned out to be popular and very useful since its adoption last May.
Mr. Speaker, I find that the amendments the House brought to the Farm Credit Act in May 1975 really encourage young people to settle or stay in agriculture, and the figures I produced demonstrate this. Consequently, I think that the proposals in the motion before the House would not really improve the rural economy.
April 30, 1976

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED INCENTIVES FOR YOUNG FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words about the motion on which I agree in principle. However, in view of the present economic conditions. I think it is impossible for the Farm Credit Corporation to increase its funds at the same pace as it thought it would. Actually, the corporation will not have enough funds to approve the same amount of credit as for 1975-76. In addition, since it had to carry certain amounts involved last year over its budget for this year, it is evident that the number of new loans should be reduced likewise.
I think that we should also urge farmers to take part in the anti-inflation program, much as we ask all groups in our society and all our industrial sectors to do. However I think that with all the new guidelines concerning farm credit it will be possible for us, while beating inflation, to reach certain goals.
Those aims have, I believe, been clearly defined in the criteria outlined by the Department of Agriculture. I am quoting only a few instances of the consolidation of applicants' debts. Formerly, it was possible for a farmer to gather all his debts and apply for a single loan which would take care of all the total indebtedness. Now we shall urge instead other loan companies to lend the money so that the corporation may pursue its activities and its aim of improving the agricultural production in this country. This is why we must earmark funds for those farmers who do not derive an adequate income from their operation and who wish to buy more land.
We shall not lend money so readily to those farmers who have enough land, assets and an adequate income.
Those who do not have enough land to farm are unable to derive an adequate income from farming will be particularly encouraged.
Moreover, we will give assistance to the younger people-and I often hear this comment in my constituency- because a young farmer today does not have enough money to buy land which costs more and more. Thus, we will grant loans particularly to one, two or three members of the same family who want to buy the family farm.
Mr. Speaker, I think that even though fewer will be available for farm credit, it will still be possible to help the farmers who either wish to improve their lot or simply to take up farming. In my opinion, this is one aspect of the problem facing the young farmers and those who are developing their operation.
We should not be concerned only with financing problems facing farmers but I believe that with provincial and perhaps even municipal authorities we should hold a joint meeting of the three levels of government with a view to constituting agricultural land banks.
In an area such as mine, even if farm credit is available to the farmers, it has become unthinkable to buy land
Farm Credit Act
because most if not all of it has passed into the hands of speculators. Even if he has already settled, a farmer cannot think of increasing his land, let alone a young man who intends to enter this industry. Therefore I believe the major problem does not exist at the credit level only but also extends to the possiblity of acquiring land.
Mr. Speaker, if we do not stop this shameful speculation which is now raging in the Montreal area, we will lose all the best agricultural land in Quebec.
I do not think we should dwell merely on the financial problem. We should rather consider the possibility now given to present and future farmers to buy new lands. And I would urge the committee on agriculture to look into this matter so as to be in a position to make recommendations to the provincial agriculture ministers and also to the municipal affairs ministers who are the only ones qualified and empowered to act in zoning matters.
Mr. Speaker, I think that if we could do as some American states have done and urge the provincial legislatures to intervene as some American states and zone certain agricultural areas, land speculation would no longer be possible in those regions.
So long as we do not come to grips with the financial problem, to earmark additional funds for the Farm Credit Corporation will only amount to overbidding.
I also think that we, as a government, should urge the lending institutions such as banks and trust companies to make more and more loans to the farmers who have always found it difficult to borrow money, and that is why they have always relied on the government. If we believe in our farming industry, I wonder why financial institutions such as banks are not more interested in this field, which proves most profitable. Unfortunately, one only has to consider the farming production surpluses last year.
Mr. Speaker, even if it is hard to tell the farmers that we cannot make more funds available to them, increase their borrowing power next year, I think they must agree to join us and the other sectors of the Canadian economy in our fight against inflation, a fight which has made a very good start with the results we already know, which gives us some hope of a decreasing rate of inflation this year.
However, Mr. Speaker, I would like to support the motion of my colleague, but with the present inflationary crisis, I have to say that however valuable this project may be, we will have to postpone it before adopting it.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED INCENTIVES FOR YOUNG FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to say that, in principle, the reasons given by the hon. member are acceptable, no doubt, but I think we must put the problem in its true perspective. On one hand, every day the government is urged to reduce its expenditures, to cut its budget, while, on the other hand we hear new demands being constantly pressed upon the government to meet certain needs.
All agree that like many other laws the Farm Credit Act could be amended, as the hon. member has said, and bettered so that we encourage our young producers. On the other hand, in view of the present situation of the dairy policy in 1976-77 for example, not only do we try to find

April 30, 1976
Farm Credit Act
incentives for the producers to produce more and improve their facilities, but at the same time, because of the current world situation, we have to ask the farmers to reduce their production.
So in a context like this, I think that at a given moment the government has had to decide that expenditures for farm credit would be curtailed. I do not think this is an attempt to hold back Canadian agriculture as a whole, but on the contrary, to rationalize its production. Even in our rural areas, where the economy is in a particularly difficult predicament due to the inflation, we still must ensure proper balance between costs and returns in agricultural production.
Almost daily we hear protests about our social legislation as the government has become the main employer in this country with such schemes as health benefits, social welfare and unemployment insurance. But I think that after having pondered on the present economic situation, we are rather led to bring back the workers to work, to try to find them new job opportunities and to stop creating and encouraging ventures which would represent far too many risks in the present conditions of our economy.
This means that the policy of the government with regard to assistance to farmers is to make sure first and foremost of the profitability of existing farm operations. On the other hand, we must really be certain now when offering farm credit that those who are eligible to it really have the ability to do the job so as to minimize lending risks for the government and to ensure maximum yield of the money that the government makes available to producers.
Therefore, it is now almost unthinkable that in its agricultural policy, the govermnent should add some so-called incentives when the priority as concerns agriculture really seems to be to stabilize and ensure profitability. I therefore consider that, in theory, the suggestion of the hon. member is acceptable. However, at this time, in view of present conditions, this subject should be referred to the committee on agriculture where it can be studied in depth while taking into account in particular rural areas which are now more likely than others to be affected by the current problems caused by inflation.
Of course, I am among those who are quite concerned by the econcomy of rural areas. Obviously an attempt must be made to save the economy of our rural areas. We can probably hope to succeed in the not too distant future, and even in the near future in reviving our rural economy, which must necessarily provide farmers with sufficient economic means.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I believe that we on this side cannot help rural economy without speaking of agricultural zoning. I know that, in this regard, the provinces have already undertaken projects which, I hope, can be realized and it is really in this sense that any amendment to the farm credit act will be truly effective and acceptable, and I would even say necessary for rural areas.
Therefore, we must definitely assess the needs of young producers. To deal with the need of young producers is also to deal with their training, because agriculture was once a venture we must now realize that the Canadian farm producer has become a true expert in his field. I think that

government members cannot take the risk of plowing huge amounts of money without making sure that prospective farm producers are equal to the task and this means having an adequate and complete training in order to ensure the survival of the farming community.
Therefore, in my view, raising the problem of farm credit amounts to actually considering on the one hand saving the economy of Canadian rural areas and on the other hand encouraging producers to make use of their personal skills and enabling them to earn an honest living. By the same token, it also amounts, for instance, to requiring from producers enough preparation and seriousness so that government loans may really be considered profitable and that risk may also be considered as really calculated.
Then, looking at the hon. member's proposal, I suggest that the committee which is now discussing the estimates has already raised the problem of a readjustment of our farm credit policy, and I think this is indeed the most appropriate and acceptable way to discuss the new farm credit policy.
Turning back especially to the developments we have been, and will be, witnessing as regards our dairy policy, it is nevertheless necessary to ask producers as well as producers' associations to make an effort at this stage so that our partners in Canadian agriculture, namely the producers themselves, may strive to rationalize their own operations and we may really believe that agriculture must be supported by the government. However, it must not become a novel form of welfare; rather it must consist of elements necessary and essential to a rural economy based on efficiency and profitability.
Now, this is also an appeal to producers themselves as well as to producers' associations to ensure that they are as serious as this government can be, and only in these conditions will the government be eventually able to grant loans which will really assist agriculture and will not simply be another form of welfare.
Then, Mr. Speaker, I think that somewhat explains the concerns we are sharing with the hon. member. On the other hand, in the present context, there is always this dilemma which we are facing: as each day come to pass we are asking more from this government while on the other hand, we are requesting at the same time that it should practise restraint. But one must realize that the government, like any other organization, must do some accounting, calculate its risks and make its decisions. And I suggest that the decision that was made recently in the area of farm credit has been at the advantage of the Canadian economy. And until further notice, we must support the government's present position unless we can demonstrate the merits of another policy.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED INCENTIVES FOR YOUNG FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, motion No. 12 proposed by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Schellenberger) and dated January 27, 1975 recommends that the government amend the Farm Credit Act to encourage young people to stay on the farm or expand their farm operations or in some cases to allow young people who left the farm because of a lack of financial means to come back.
April 30, 1976

The last amendments made by the government are giving encouragement in that direction. Mr. Speaker, as we are now aware, a person under 35 can, without leaving his job in the industrial sector, buy a farm and benefit from the Farm Credit Act.
Motion No. 12 has some good aspects. It particularly recommends an interest rate of only 5 per cent. A member of the government side mentioned that we should also take into account the case of young couples who want to buy a property. Those people will have to pay a rate higher than 5 per cent. In some cases, they can benefit from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation grants and pay a rate of 8 per cent. The suggestion has some good aspects and in certain cases that rate can apply to young farmers and not only the young but every farmer in the province of Quebec.
Another suggestion that could be considered by this government is that for a certain period the Farm Credit Corporation could, through an agreement, increase the loan of those young people without professional fees. It is another suggestion that could be considered by the government. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) responsible to Parliament for the Farm Credit Corporation announced in a press release this week that the funds available for 1976-77 would not be as high as for 1975-76; one of the reasons alleged by the minister is the following: For 1975-76, the Farm Credit Corporation loaned upwards of $600 million, or made loan commitments that will be considered in 1976-77 and in such cases we have, as it is called mortgaged the available appropriations for 1976 and 1977.
In various instances in the past, the government took measures to help young farmers expand their operations. This provided increased loan opportunities where two or three people get into a partnership to continue the family operation. Hon. members are aware that the average age figure among the farmers is relatively high. I understand the most recent statistics show the age to be above 50, and the Farm Credit Act amendment has allowed the senior farmer to indirectly carry on farming, while allowing one or two sons to take over the operation.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with deference and respect, I do not know whether in the circumstances you can say the private members' hour has expired. Standing Order 4 states that the House adjourns at five o'clock on Fridays. I look at the clock and it is only 3:20. If the opponents to the point of view which I am putting forward say that there was unanimous consent, I have to say there was unanimous consent only to part of the matter that would allow us to continue to the actual time of 3.20 o'clock.
The unanimous consent that was given when Your Honour was not in the Chair was to call if four o'clock at that time so that private members' business could continue. However, there was no attempt at that time, nor was it asked that there be unanimous consent that the House
Time of Adjournment
adjourn at the end of an hour. Therefore we are now stuck with the Standing Orders of the House.
In view of all the circumstances I do not believe Your Honour could properly rule, and I gather you have not ruled, that private members' hour has adjourned.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED INCENTIVES FOR YOUNG FARMERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I point out that the Standing Orders do not say that private members' business shall be for 60 minutes-for one hour. The Standing Orders say that private members' business shall be from four o'clock to five o'clock. It so happens that at 2.20 this afternoon, eastern daylight time, we decided by unanimous consent that it was four o'clock. So private members' business lasts from that point until five o'clock. It is not yet five o'clock, not even in Newfoundland where things are always half an hour later. There is nothing in the book which says it is an hour. The book says it shall be from four o'clock to five o'clock. Joshua made the sun stand still a long time ago. We have not done the same thing. We pushed the sun back a bit. But there has been no unanimous consent to call it five o'clock at 3.20. If the government wishes to make a motion to adjourn, that is a different story, but I do not think we can now decide it is five o'clock unless there is unanimous consent.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED INCENTIVES FOR YOUNG FARMERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am really surprised by the remarks of the hon. member who spoke before me, considering what was said in this House during the past few years. At 2.20 it was unanimously agreed to call it 4 o'clock. The hon. member says he cannot stop the sun, but everyone can very well stop his watch or move it forward. I suggest this is exactly what this House did at 2:20, when we unanimously agreed to call it 4 o'clock. It does not matter much where the sun lies for that matter. We call it 4 o'clock, we move on to 4 o'clock. There has to be some consistency in this House. If we unanimously call it 4 o'clock, one hour later it has to be 5 o'clock.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader

speechtext: When the Deputy Chairman of Committees was in the chair there was some discussion about business for this afternoon and I recall saying that in order to bring about the adjournment of the House on June 30 it was undesirable to open discussion on measures which do not appear on the order paper. Following this the Chair, as I recall the words, asked "Do we hafe unanimous consent to call it four o'clock?" It was my understanding that what we had agreed to was to advance the clock and I suggest it would be ridiculous on our part to turn it back now. The implication was that we had come to the end of the day and were beginning the private members' hour by advancing the clock to four o'clock. If we were to take any other point of view, then at four o'clock we would have to call it four o'clock twice, and that would be ridiculous.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED INCENTIVES FOR YOUNG FARMERS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED INCENTIVES FOR YOUNG FARMERS
speechtext:
I do understand the preoccupation of the hon. member. Recalling what was said when by unanimous consent the House decided at 2.19 to call it four o'clock, I have to consider the situation in the perspective of the decision made at that time. The Chair has to judge

Time of Adjournment
not the intent of hon. members now, but the intention which was in their minds when they agreed to call it four o'clock.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) said, and I agree with him, that nowhere does the Standing Order say that the private members' hour shall last 60 minutes. Such words do not appear. But we can see from Standing Order 15(4) that the time allotted for private members' business every day is either from five o'clock to six o'clock or from four o'clock to five o'clock on Friday, which is the equivalent of 60 minutes. Hon. members want the Chair to decide that this hour should, today, last two hours and 41 minutes. I do not think the Chair can do this. They have heard me say that the hour provided for the consideration of private members' business has expired. That is the form which has been in use here ever since I have been in the House, either in the chair or as a private member. To me, that hour is 60 minutes in principle.
Hon. members should also consider the fact that they do on occasion recognize that the length of time allotted to private members' business is 60 minutes even though it
might only last for 15 minutes. Moreover, if it is the wish of the House, private members' business can be extended. What is being suggested now could be done only by unanimous consent. Hon. members are asking the Chair, in the absence of unanimous consent, to say that the hour allotted to private members' business should extend to two hours and 41 minutes. This cannot be done by the Chair alone; it could be done only with the consent of all hon. members.
The hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier) said it has always been recognized, in recent times at least, that when hon. members decide to advance the private members' hour, it is understood that the time allotted for that portion of our business will be 60 minutes. So my interpretation of the situation, in the light of the precedents and taking into account the unanimous agreement which was reached at 2.19 to call it four o'clock, and reading in that decision the intention to proceed with the private members' hour for the time normally allotted, that is, for one hour, is that I have to call it five o'clock. And I do call it five o'clock.
Accordingly, the House stands adjourned until Monday at 2 p.m. under the terms of Standing Order 2(1).
At 3.31 p.m. the House adjourned, without question put, pursuant to Standing Order.

Monday, May 3, 1976
